newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW-Dutch quietly upbeat on new EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Dutch quietly upbeat on new EU treaty.

text.p: The Netherlands is cautiously upbeat on its chances of rounding off the inter-governmental conference (IGC) on the European Union treaty review, Dutch deputy foreign minister Michiel Patijn said on Friday.
"I am not pessimistic about our chances...Europe's political leadership knows only too well what is at stake if (IGC) is not concluded on schedule," Patijn said in an interview.
Patijn will take over the chair of the IGC negotiating group when The Netherlands assumes the six-month EU presidency on January 1.
Delays in finalising a new-look Maastricht Treaty would inevitably push back decision-making on the admission of new members to the 15-country alliance, he said.
"Politically this would be very difficult to justify."

If treaty review negotiations drag on beyond next summer, ratification by the various member parliaments could be thrown into disarray by French and German general elections in 1998, in which Europe is expected to be a key issue.
"We must avoid a situation in which (treaty) ratification coincides with the decision on (which members will take part in) Economic and Monetary Union.
"I think this will put sufficient political pressure on the parties to enable us to get a result," Patijn said.
But the Netherlands would not seek to complete the treaty review at any price, he warned.

"It must have a minimum quality as regards efficiency, democracy and effectiveness...It must be able to serve as a basis for an enlarged European Union into the 21st century and offer sufficient leeway for innovation," he said.
Many existing EU procedures are too unwieldy for an enlarged alliance, but member states are still divided on key issues of decision-making and influence.
"The biggest hurdles are likely to be the future composition of the European Commission and qualified majority voting," Patijn said.

The Dutch, whose consensus politics have spawned a string of largely stable coalition governments, are keen proponents of qualified majority voting and would like to see it extended to a range of areas which currently require unanimity.
"Too many constitutionally lightweight decisions needlessly require unanimous approval...in an enlarged community it will become increasingly difficult to make any decisions at all," Patijn said.

Areas ripe for majority decision-making include foreign policy issues unrelated to the military, and immigration, visa and asylum policy which should be regulated on a community-wide level, Patijn said.

"Everything to do with asylum, visa and immigration policy -- which is effectively an extension of the functioning of the internal market -- should eventually be able to be decided by qualified majority voting, either in this treaty or at a later date," he said. "We are very much in favour (of that)."
But he said Britain's objections to communal decision-making on immigration would have to be accommodated by means of a 'tailor-made' solution.
However, the Dutch have no intention of accommodating Britain's stand-alone position on the treaty's social chapter regulating community labour rights.
"The social chapter is intended as part of the central market and it is flawed when member states have an opt-out -- we want to correct that flaw," Patijn said.
Britain's opposition leader Tony Blair has already pledged to sign up to the social chapter if his Labour Party wins general elections due to be held no later than May.
